problem: Existing visual navigation uses image or waypoint goals and closed-loop feedback, and world models for navigation (NWM, PathDreamer) focus on visual prediction decoupled from policy and ignore language. Unified autoregressive approaches (UniWM) need inefficient interleaved training and inference.
motivation: Language conveys intent and context that image goals cannot. Open-loop language-conditioned navigation from a single starting observation directly probes predictive planning and allows offline evaluation without simulators. This calls for models that couple language grounding, imagination and policy learning.
key_idea: Introduce the open-loop language-conditioned visual navigation task and LCVN dataset, and solve it with two agent families: a language-conditioned diffusion world model (LCVN-WM) paired with a latent actor-critic (LCVN-AC), and a unified autoregressive MLLM (LCVN-Uni) that predicts action and next observation in one pass.
insight: Language instructions act as the goal specification: removing them consistently lowers SR and imagination quality (LCVN-WM w/o ins SR 0.35 vs 0.43 on val seen). Condition importance ranks action > language > time (Table ablation). The diffusion WM is better at imagination and seen-scene control, while the unified AR agent generalizes better to unseen environments (val unseen SR 0.27 vs 0.19), suggesting shared representation of planning and prediction helps under distribution shift. Landmark-style instructions work best, and latent-space modeling beats pixel-space.
method: LCVN task and dataset: open-loop generation of the full action sequence from one egocentric RGB observation plus an instruction; 39,016 trajectories, 117,048 instructions in Concise/Intricate/Landmark styles, built from Go Stanford, ReCon, SCAND, HuRoN and TartanDrive (unseen), with Qwen-VL-2.5 generation plus human refinement.

LCVN-WM: a DiT with cross-attention to frozen CLIP text embeddings in every block (LDiT), action/time-shift/diffusion-timestep conditioning via AdaLN, VAE latents (32x32), trained with Diffusion Forcing (independent per-frame noise levels).

LCVN-AC: actor-critic trained entirely in the frozen WM latent space. A CVAE latent plan is aligned between expert and learner encoders by KL divergence, and a cosine-similarity intrinsic reward compares imagined and expert latents. The critic regresses to λ-returns, and the actor adds KL and CLIP-style instruction alignment losses.

LCVN-Uni: Anole-7B (Chameleon-style) fine-tuned with LoRA; VQ image, BPE text and bin action tokenizers; jointly predicts next action bins and next observation tokens in one forward pass with L_plan + λ L_imagine.
Inference: LCVN-WM imagines the next latent state, LCVN-AC outputs the action, and the loop repeats until a stop action; LCVN-Uni feeds its own predicted observation back as input.
Baselines: Diamond, NWM and NWM (lang), each paired with a separately trained LCVN-AC.

setting.backbone: LCVN-WM: DiT-XL (~1B) + CLIP text encoder + ImageVAE, with LCVN-AC actor-critic; LCVN-Uni: Anole-7B fine-tuned with LoRA
setting.training_data: LCVN train split (28,813 trajectories / 86,439 instructions) from Go Stanford, ReCon, SCAND, HuRoN; optional Ego4D in an ablation
setting.observation: single initial egocentric RGB image plus language instruction; afterwards only self-imagined observations
setting.action_space: continuous (dx, dy, dyaw) per step with a stop action; discretized into bin tokens for LCVN-Uni
setting.privileged: none (the ground-truth action sequence is used for imagination-quality rollout evaluation only)

numbers_note: Results are only on the authors' own LCVN benchmark (SR reported as fractions 0-1, e.g. 0.42 = 42%). Imagination metrics (SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS/DreamSim) are in Tables 2 and ablations and are not listed here.
results: On LCVN, LCVN-WM+LCVN-AC gets the best val-seen SR (0.43) and LCVN-Uni the best val-unseen (0.27) and test (0.36) SR, versus the strongest baseline NWM (lang)+LCVN-AC (0.29 / 0.13 / 0.22). LCVN-WM also gives the best imagination (PSNR 20.316 at k=4 vs 11.612 for NWM (lang)) and is faster per step than NWM and LCVN-Uni (6.4 s vs 11.2 s and 20.5 s).
limitations: Evaluation only on the authors' own offline dataset with pre-recorded real-robot trajectories, with no closed-loop or real-robot deployment and SR defined loosely (within an average step size)
Open-loop imagination accumulates errors, and both agents have low absolute SR on unseen environments (≤0.27)
Inference is slow (LCVN-Uni 20.5 s/step, LCVN-WM 6.4 s), and Anole-7B's fixed 4096-token window forces a resolution/context tradeoff
